title: Why Hard Lessons Are Good For Your Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/11/10/why-hard-lessons-are-good-for-your-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes the tough call of canceling a special lesson or activity when students show they've taken it, and the teacher, for granted. He argues that such 'hard lessons' can be the best medicine for a classroom, restoring balance to what should be a two-way relationship between teacher and students. Allowing complacency to slide, he explains, signals that mediocrity and disrespect are acceptable, while a hard lesson reasserts that excellence is expected. He recommends delivering the consequence with minimal explanation, letting the disappointment itself do the teaching, since lecturing dilutes its impact. The piece closes with a vivid image of a teacher calmly canceling a science lesson, illustrating how brief, decisive action leaves a lasting impression.
points: Canceling a special lesson or activity when students take it for granted restores balance in a lopsided teacher-student relationship.
Accepting complacency signals that mediocrity and disrespect are tolerated; hard lessons reassert that excellence is expected.
Hard lessons should be delivered with minimal explanation, letting the disappointment itself do the teaching.
After a hard lesson, students typically respond with sharper listening and quicker compliance going forward.
The lost lesson can usually be rescheduled — the point is the impact of the moment, not permanently forfeiting the content.
quotes: Whether it’s canceling a cool science experiment, a special activity, a holiday party, or an outdoor learning game, hard lessons—those that profoundly disappoint students—can be the best medicine for your classroom.
Hard lessons send the message to your students that your classroom is a two-way street. You give your best for them. That’s a given.
When you let things go, when you accept less than what your students are capable of, in effect you’re telling them that mediocrity is okay, disrespect is tolerated, and half-efforts are acceptable.
Hard lessons, both for individuals and whole classrooms, result in a humbler attitude more attuned and eager to make amends.
Hard lessons are best left for your students to process on their own. So avoid explaining, lecturing, or trying to tell them how they should feel.
Because of your behavior today—walking into class noisily, following directions poorly, side-talking—I’m canceling the science lesson.
